reviews.text: The new Apple MacBook Neo is a stunning machine with a 14.2-inch Retina display that boasts incredible brightness. Powered by the M4 Pro chip, it handles heavy video editing tasks without any lag or overheating issues. However, the 8GB of RAM feels limiting for power users who run multiple virtual machines simultaneously. I also noticed that the battery life drops significantly when using the GPU for extended rendering sessions. At $2,499, the price point is steep, though the build quality and keyboard feel justify the cost for professionals.

The new MacBook Neo feels incredibly light and the aluminum chassis is built with premium quality. Its 3000x2000 display is stunningly bright even in direct sunlight, and the M4 Pro CPU handles video editing without a stutter. However, the battery life is only about 8 hours with heavy usage, which is disappointing for a device in this price range. The keyboard feels solid but the touchpad is a bit too small for my liking during long work sessions. Overall, it is a capable machine, though the lack of an SD card slot is an annoying omission for photographers.

The new MacBook Neo with 32GB of RAM feels incredibly fast for my video editing work. Its stunning 3K display is bright enough to use outdoors, though the price is quite steep. It is a solid machine, but the lack of extra ports means I need dongles.

I am amazed by the battery life, which easily lasts a full 14-hour workday even with the 1200-nit display turned on. However, the price of $2,499 for this configuration feels a bit steep compared to the previous model. The keyboard feels tactile and responsive, making long typing sessions comfortable without any fatigue. I do wish it had more USB-A ports, as I still rely on older dongles for my external drives.

The laptop is incredibly light and portable, fitting perfectly into my small backpack for daily commutes. The screen is gorgeous with vibrant colors, but the touchpad occasionally feels a bit too smooth and slippery. Battery drain seems inconsistent when running multiple heavy applications simultaneously. It is a solid machine overall, though I am not entirely convinced it justifies the premium cost. The build quality is excellent, with the aluminum chassis feeling durable and premium to the touch.

At this price point, I expected more Thunderbolt ports, yet the inclusion of only two ports limits connectivity options. At $2,299, the price is steep, but the build quality and aluminum unibody feel premium. I appreciate the MagSafe charging port and two Thunderbolt 5 connections, though the lack of an SD card slot is inconvenient. The keyboard is responsive and comfortable for long typing sessions, and macOS Sonoma runs smoothly without lag.
